analysis.one_liner: Requires advance reports to Congress before any U.S. negotiation that would weaken patent, copyright, or trademark rights.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees on November 8, 2024 and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President and any U.S. trade negotiator to give the House and Senate Judiciary Committees a report at least 60 days before starting negotiations on any international agreement that would reduce the value, scope, or enforceability of U.S. patents, copyrights, plant variety rights, trademarks, or trade secrets. The report would have to analyze the impact on U.S. intellectual property holders and on the U.S. intellectual property system. It would not change any patent or copyright law directly; its practical effect would be to add notice and analysis before the United States could negotiate away intellectual property protections, such as the international waivers of drug patents discussed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets — industries like brand-name pharmaceuticals, entertainment, software, and agricultural seed companies — would gain a procedural shield: any U.S. negotiation to loosen those rights abroad would first have to be documented and analyzed for Congress. Congress itself would gain advance visibility into trade negotiations affecting intellectual property.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent and copyright holders, led by brand-name drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President or any U.S. negotiator to submit a report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees at least 60 days before negotiating any international agreement that would reduce or restrict the value, scope, or enforceability of a patent right, with quantitative and qualitative analysis of the potential outcomes.
Applies the same reporting requirement to copyright, plant variety rights, trademarks, and trade secrets, covering five categories of intellectual property in one bill.
Defines 'United States person' broadly to include U.S. corporations, so the impact analysis must cover rights held by U.S. companies as well as individuals.

analysis.who_pays: If the reporting requirement made the United States slower or more reluctant to negotiate intellectual property waivers, the cost would fall on patients and consumers who rely on generic or cheaper versions of protected products, and on U.S. negotiators' flexibility in trade talks. Taxpayers would also bear the cost of producing the required analyses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients seeking cheaper generics and U.S. trade negotiators

drawbacks.text: The requirement is one-directional: it demands notice and analysis only for agreements that would weaken intellectual property rights, not for agreements that would strengthen them, so it adds friction to one side of trade policy without a symmetric oversight benefit.

A 60-day advance reporting mandate could delay or chill U.S. participation in international agreements to ease intellectual property protections — for example, the kind of patent waiver negotiated during the COVID-19 pandemic to expand access to medicines — which matters most in public health emergencies.
The bill creates no new rights for consumers; its benefit is procedural and its practical value depends entirely on whether Congress acts on the reports it receives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine case for the transparency goal: Congress currently learns about intellectual property concessions in trade talks after the fact. But the bill is designed asymmetrically — it only slows negotiations that reduce intellectual property protections, never ones that expand them — and its main practical effect would be to make it harder for the United States to agree to waivers that lower prices of protected goods, particularly medicines. The oversight benefit is modest; the cost, if it deterred waiver negotiations, would fall on patients and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary and Agriculture Committees after referral and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, never receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Darrell Issa introduced the bill in the House on November 8, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress, with one other original cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, additionally, to the House Agriculture Committee.
Two House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no further action was taken.

The bill's short title, the 'TRIPS Waivers Act,' ties it to the World Trade Organization's agreement on trade-related intellectual property rights, the treaty whose waivers the reporting requirement would cover.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, since the bill never moved. Generic-drug makers, patients, and U.S. negotiators who could benefit from future intellectual property waivers are better off that the hurdle was never enacted; patent and copyright holders lost a procedural protection they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Future waiver beneficiaries; IP holders gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were House Republicans, and no Democrat supported it; no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape comes only from sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill is aimed at negotiations like the TRIPS waiver process, in which countries have sought to relax patent protections to expand access to generic medicines. Requiring a 60-day advance report and impact analysis before any such negotiation would make waivers harder to strike quietly, protecting patent revenue at the expense of patients seeking cheaper drugs.

industries.industry: Entertainment, publishing, and software copyright holders
industries.note: The bill would give copyright holders advance notice and an impact analysis before any U.S. agreement that weakens copyright abroad. Stronger copyright protection does not always run against the public, but the reporting hurdle only applies to agreements reducing copyright, tilting future negotiations toward the industry's position.

Plant variety rights are covered by the bill, so any U.S. negotiation to ease plant breeders' rights protections abroad would first require a report to Congress. This protects seed industry revenue but could slow international agreements affecting farmers' access to varieties.
